claims.title: Forbidden request returns a server error (5xx) on GET /account
claims.evidence: GET /account with an invalid bearer token returned HTTP 500 instead of a clean 401/403. An unauthorized request must be denied, not crash the server — a 5xx here leaks internals and hides real faults.

remediation.why: A forbidden request crashes with a 5xx instead of a clean 401/403, leaking internals and making real faults indistinguishable from unauthorized traffic.
remediation.fix: Handle authentication/authorization failures explicitly: return 401 (not authenticated) or 403 (not permitted) before any work that can throw, and never let the auth layer fall through to an unhandled 500.

claims.title: OS command injection via query param 'host' on /ping
claims.evidence: GET /ping with 'host'='127.0.0.1;echo qaxcmdfcfade7cc4' executed an injected shell command (its output was reflected; HTTP 200). User input reaches a shell without sanitisation — full remote code execution.

remediation.why: User input reaches an OS shell, so an attacker can run arbitrary commands on the server — full remote code execution and host compromise.
remediation.fix: Never pass user input to a shell. Call the program directly with an argument array (no shell), validate against a strict allow-list, and drop shell metacharacters; avoid system()/exec with a composed string.

claims.title: CORS reflects an arbitrary Origin with credentials
claims.evidence: Request to / with Origin: https://qax-cors-probe.example was answered with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://qax-cors-probe.example and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. The app trusts any site's origin, so a malicious page can make cross-origin requests and read the victim's authenticated responses.

remediation.why: The app reflects any caller's Origin in Access-Control-Allow-Origin, so a malicious website can make cross-origin requests to this API — and with credentials enabled, read the victim's authenticated responses.
remediation.fix: Allow only an explicit allow-list of trusted origins; never reflect the request Origin, and never combine a wildcard/reflected origin with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.

claims.title: Stack trace / internal error disclosed on GET /items/{item_id}
claims.evidence: An error on /items/{item_id} returned a raw stack trace / framework internals (HTTP 500), disclosing source paths and implementation detail that aid an attacker. Errors should be generic.

remediation.why: An error exposes an interactive debugger / stack trace, leaking source and internals — the console can lead to remote code execution.
remediation.fix: Disable debug mode in deployed environments and return generic error responses; log details server-side only.

claims.title: Unknown routes return a server error (5xx) instead of 404
claims.evidence: GET /qax_nonexistent_38f81eb1823b/does/not/exist — a path that cannot exist — returned HTTP 500. Unknown routes should return 404; a 5xx pollutes monitoring and makes real faults and scans indistinguishable from crashes.

remediation.why: Unknown routes return a server error (5xx) instead of 404, which pollutes monitoring and hides real faults.
remediation.fix: Add proper 404/405 handlers so unknown paths and methods return a clean 4xx.

claims.title: Host header reflected into a URL on GET /reset-link
claims.evidence: A forged Host 'qaxc1df7e805a.evil.invalid' was used by the server to build a URL in the response body on GET /reset-link. An attacker can set the Host of a victim's request to poison password-reset links and the web cache.

remediation.why: The app builds URLs (reset links, redirects, cache keys) from the incoming Host header, so an attacker can poison password-reset emails and the web cache.
remediation.fix: Never trust the Host/X-Forwarded-Host header for URL generation. Use a configured canonical base URL, and validate Host against an allowlist.

claims.title: Open redirect via 'url' on /redirect
claims.evidence: GET /redirect?url=https://qax-redirect.example/evil responded 302 with Location: https://qax-redirect.example/evil — the app redirects to an attacker-controlled external host taken straight from the request parameter.

remediation.why: A redirect target is taken from a request parameter without validation, so an attacker can send victims to a site they control (phishing, OAuth token theft).
remediation.fix: Redirect only to an allow-list of known internal paths/hosts; reject absolute external URLs, or map a redirect key to a server-side URL table.

claims.title: Path traversal / local file read via query param 'file' on /download
claims.evidence: GET /download?file=/etc/passwd returned an OS file's contents (HTTP 200; matched /etc/passwd or win.ini). The parameter builds a filesystem path without sanitisation.

remediation.why: A path parameter is used to build a filesystem path without sanitisation, so an attacker can read files outside the web root (e.g. /etc/passwd, secrets, source) — and sometimes write them.
remediation.fix: Never pass user input to file paths directly: map it to an allow-list of known names/ids, reject '..' and absolute paths, and resolve+confirm the final path stays under the intended base directory.

claims.title: Search rejects an ordinary character with HTTP 405 on GET /search
claims.evidence: On GET /search a benign term in 'q' returned 200, but the character '@' returned HTTP 405. Real searches (emails, slash-separated terms) contain these characters; an unsanitised query syntax rejects them instead of escaping them.

remediation.why: A search/filter input returns a raw 405/5xx on an ordinary character, so real queries (emails, slash-separated terms) fail — an unsanitised query-operator syntax is rejecting input it should escape.
remediation.fix: Escape or parameterise user input before it reaches the search/query engine, and return 0 results (not an error) for a term that matches nothing.

claims.title: Response security headers missing: X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options / CSP frame-ancestors, Content-Security-Policy
claims.evidence: The app root (HTTP 500) did not set: X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options / CSP frame-ancestors, Content-Security-Policy. These are defence-in-depth against clickjacking, MIME-sniffing and XSS.

remediation.why: Standard response security headers are missing, removing defence-in-depth against clickjacking, MIME-sniffing, protocol downgrade and XSS.
remediation.fix: Set Strict-Transport-Security (HTTPS), X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, X-Frame-Options/CSP frame-ancestors, and a Content-Security-Policy — e.g. via a security-headers middleware.

claims.title: SQL injection in GET /products/{pid} (path param 'pid')
claims.evidence: A " in path param 'pid' produced a SQL error (benign → 404, payload → 500). The input reaches a raw, unparameterized query.

remediation.why: User input reaches a raw SQL query, allowing data theft, auth bypass, or data destruction.
remediation.fix: Use parameterized queries / ORM bindings (e.g. WHERE x = ?) — never build SQL by string concatenation or f-strings with user input.

claims.title: SSRF via query param 'url' on /fetch
claims.evidence: GET /fetch with 'url' set to a URL under our control caused the server to make an outbound request to it (confirmed by an out-of-band callback). An attacker can make the server reach internal services, cloud metadata, or arbitrary hosts.

remediation.why: The server fetches a URL supplied by the client, so an attacker can make it reach internal-only services, cloud metadata endpoints (credentials), or arbitrary hosts — a pivot into the internal network.
remediation.fix: Validate the URL against an allow-list of hosts/schemes, resolve and block private/link-local IP ranges (incl. redirects), disable unused URL schemes (file/gopher), and send outbound fetches through an egress proxy.

claims.title: Server-side template injection via query param 'name' on /greet
claims.evidence: A template expression in 'name' on GET /greet was EVALUATED server-side: {{256*947}} rendered as 242432 (and a prior expression rendered as 497652). The literal expression did not appear — user input reaches a template engine, which is typically RCE.

remediation.why: User input is concatenated into a server-side template and evaluated, so an attacker can run template/engine code — typically a path to RCE.
remediation.fix: Never build templates from user input. Render a fixed template and pass user data as bound variables/context only; if dynamic templates are truly needed, use a sandboxed engine and a strict allowlist.

claims.title: Collection GET /logs returns an unbounded, unpaginated list
claims.evidence: GET /logs returned 150 rows in one response and ignored a limit=1 request (still 150 rows). An unbounded list grows without limit as data accumulates — slow payloads, heavy DOM, and a denial-of-service lever.

remediation.why: A collection endpoint returns its whole table in one response and ignores a limit parameter — the payload and client DOM grow without bound as data accumulates, a performance and denial-of-service risk.
remediation.fix: Paginate every collection endpoint (limit/offset or cursor) with a sane default and a hard maximum page size; never return an unbounded array.

claims.title: Reflected XSS via query param 'name' on /greet
claims.evidence: GET /greet reflected the markup <qax3c0eba0d40> verbatim (unencoded) into an HTML response. Script in 'name' would execute in the victim's browser — the output is not HTML-encoded.

remediation.why: User input is reflected into the page without encoding, so an attacker can run script in victims' browsers — session theft, account takeover, and actions performed as the victim.
remediation.fix: Context-aware output encoding (HTML/attribute/JS) on every reflected value, a strict Content-Security-Policy, and a template engine that auto-escapes; never build HTML by string concatenation of raw input.
